summary.text: 字 is traditionally analyzed as 子, a child, beneath 宀, a roof; 子 is also assigned a sound role. Today it commonly means “written character.”

formation.text: The traditional analysis is phonosemantic: 宀 depicts a roof or indoor setting, while 子 depicts the child and also supplies a sound cue. This construction is an old explanation of the graph, and its graphic interpretation has been challenged.

components.text: In the traditional analysis, 宀 depicts the roof or indoor setting around the child; this interpretation has been challenged.
子 depicts the child in the traditional scene and is also assigned a sound role.

sound_limitation.text: The Old Chinese comparison is compatible with a sound role, but its exact dataset entries are reported from a local copy. The modern Mandarin pair does not establish an ancient sound relation.

sound.text: These reported Old Chinese forms have compatible consonant correspondences, though the comparison alone does not prove the graphic analysis.
The modern Mandarin readings are comparable, but do not establish the ancient relation.

history.text: A bronze-form account describes 子 below 宀. A catalog lists a Shang-period rubbing associated with 字父己觶, but that listing does not establish the inscription’s reading or make it the earliest attestation.
The traditional graphic analysis has been challenged, but the reported alternative is not detailed. No evidence identifies graphic corruption or miscopying.

uncertainties.text: The child-under-a-roof construction is a transmitted historical explanation; the reported disagreement is not detailed enough here to assess competing analyses.

senses.period: Han lexicographic account; earlier dating unresolved
senses.text: A Han lexicographic account gives birth or nurture as meanings, but does not establish when they arose or whether they represent one original sense.
字 commonly means a written character; the earliest use of this sense is not dated here.
“Word” is also a recorded meaning, but its chronology and relation to birth or nurture are unresolved.

developments.text: A later commentary links birth to nurture and then to written characters; a separate-root or derivation-from-producing account is also given. The proposed relationship and its chronology remain unresolved.

limitations.text: The Han-era explanation that written forms multiply and dictionary glosses do not independently establish the chronology or development of these meanings.

overview.text: 字 is traditionally explained as a child (子) beneath a roof (宀); 子 also supplies a sound cue. Today it commonly means “written character.”

components.text: In the traditional scene, the roof sets an indoor setting around the child.
子 is the child in the traditional scene and is also assigned a sound role.

takeaway.text: The old explanation links birth and nurture with written characters, but the development and chronology remain unresolved.

relationships.text: In the traditional construction, 宀 depicts the roof or indoor setting in the proposed child-under-a-roof scene.
In the traditional construction, 子 depicts the child beneath the roof.

The traditional account assigns 子 a sound role. Reported Old Chinese forms have compatible consonant correspondences, though the exact dataset entries are reported from a local copy. Modern Mandarin 子 zǐ and 字 zì are comparable but do not establish the ancient relation.
